findings.summary: The caption promises ten pages and two topics that the seven-title deck does not contain.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages on the four arguments, the default resolver ... and how one non-null field can null your whole response." Titles array has 7 entries, ending at "Context, Auth, Per-Request State (cont.)" with no null-propagation page.
findings.fix: Either add the missing pages (null propagation / non-null error bubbling) to reach ten, or rewrite the caption to "Seven pages on the four arguments, the default resolver that quietly runs most of your schema, why root mutations are the spec's only ordering guarantee, and the per-request context every resolver shares."

findings.summary: The footer tag chip is clipped by the bottom edge of the canvas, cutting off the lower half of its border and glyphs.
findings.evidence: "#dev #notes 2/2" sits at y≈1428 on a 1440px-tall page; its rounded border has no bottom stroke and the descenders are sliced, whereas the same chip on pages 1 and 3–7 is fully enclosed and sits ~90–190px above the bottom edge.
findings.fix: Reduce page-2 column content height (the left column runs to y≈1345 with the "// WRONG: args lands in the parent slot" code block) or shrink the body/leading for that slide so the footer chip renders inside the safe area with the same bottom margin as the other pages.

findings.summary: The term "N+1" is used as a known concept on page 3 but is not defined until page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 3 bullet: "200 `Post.title` calls is N+1 in its native habitat" — the definition ("One query for the list, one per item for the child") does not appear until the "The N+1 Shape" section on page 7.
findings.fix: On page 3, expand the bullet to define the shape inline the first time it appears, e.g. "200 `Post.title` calls — one list query plus one query per item: that is N+1", and keep page 7's section as the fix rather than the definition.

findings.summary: The fan-out table asserts 20 and 200 call counts with no stated premise for how many users or posts exist.
findings.evidence: The table rows `["Query.users","1"], ["User.name","20"], ["User.posts","20"], ["Post.title","200"]` follow a code block that shows only a singular `Query.user  => { id: 7, name: 'Ada' }`; the numbers 20 users and 10 posts each are never stated anywhere on the page.
findings.fix: Add a one-line premise directly above the table, e.g. a heading or paragraph "20 users, 10 posts each", or label the table "Query.users returns 20 users, each with 10 posts" so the 20 and 200 are derivable.

findings.summary: A `Date` returned into a `String` field does not serialize to ISO text — graphql-js calls `valueOf()` first, so it becomes the epoch-millisecond number as a string.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["a `Date`","ISO string coercion"]; sidebox: "A `Date` in a `String` field silently becomes ISO text". graphql-js `serializeObject` is `if (typeof outputValue.valueOf === 'function') { const valueOfResult = outputValue.valueOf(); if (!isObjectLike(valueOfResult)) return valueOfResult; } if (typeof outputValue.toJSON === 'function') return outputValue.toJSON();` — `Date.prototype.valueOf()` returns a number, so `toJSON()` (the ISO path) is never reached, and `GraphQLString.serialize` then returns `coercedValue.toString()` for that finite number.
findings.fix: Change the table row to ["a `Date`","epoch-ms string, e.g. `'1757000000000'`"] and the sidebox line to "A `Date` in a `String` field silently becomes its epoch-millisecond timestamp, not ISO text — `valueOf()` wins over `toJSON()`". The following line ("Declare a custom scalar instead of leaning on coercion") still stands.

findings.summary: Non-null error propagation is asserted on pages 4 and 5 and promised in the caption, but is never explained anywhere in the deck.
findings.evidence: Page 4 table row: `["missing, typed `String!`","error, propagates up"]`; page 5 bullet: "`completeValue` unwraps non-null, iterates lists, recurses, serializes leaves"; caption: "Ten pages on ... how one non-null field can null your whole response" — yet the deck contains 7 pages and no section on errors or nullability.
findings.fix: Add the errors/nullability page the caption promises (nullable field errors → null, non-null errors propagate to the nearest nullable ancestor) before or immediately after page 4, or, if the deck is meant to end at page 7, cut "error, propagates up" down to "error" and correct the caption's page count and its nullability promise.

findings.summary: The claim that every Promise at a level is awaited before the next level begins is false — graphql-js descends into each field's children as soon as that field's own Promise settles, with no per-level barrier.
findings.evidence: "Every Promise at a level is awaited before the next level" (and "Breadth-per-level, depth overall: start a level, then descend"). In `executeFields`, each `executeField` call chains its own `completeValue` — which recurses into the sub-selection — independently; `promiseForObject` only awaits siblings to assemble the result map, it does not gate child execution.
findings.fix: Replace with "Each field's Promise is awaited on its own, then that field descends — siblings never block each other", and soften the preceding bullet to "Depth-first per field; a level's siblings only rejoin when the result object is assembled".

findings.summary: Page 6 teaches dataloader lifetime rules that depend on the DataLoader definition given on page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 6: "Dataloaders MUST be built inside the context factory" and "A module-level loader serves one user's cache to another" — but what a DataLoader is, that it batches `.load(key)` calls, and that it memoizes per instance are all first explained on page 7 ("Collect every `.load(key)` in the tick, call `batchFn(keys)` once", "Memoized per instance").
findings.fix: Either move the "Per-Request Or Bust" section to page 7 after the batching/memoization explanation, or prefix it on page 6 with a one-line definition ("a DataLoader batches and caches per-key fetches for the life of its instance") so the leak rule has a stated cause.

findings.summary: The caption advertises ten pages but the set contains seven.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages on the four arguments..."; `slides` has 7 entries (pages 1–7, the last being "Context, Auth, Per-Request State (cont.)").
findings.fix: Change "Ten pages" to "Seven pages", or drop the count.

findings.summary: The #dataloader hashtag points at batching/N+1 content the deck never covers.
findings.evidence: hashtags include "#dataloader"; no title or caption line mentions batching, N+1, or DataLoader — the closest is "Execution Order And Concurrency".
findings.fix: Replace "#dataloader" with "#graphqlresolvers" (or "#apischema"), which matches the pages actually in the deck.

findings.summary: `buildSchema` takes no resolver map, so the resolver map is not "glued" at `buildSchema` time.
findings.evidence: "Two layers, glued at `makeExecutableSchema`/`buildSchema` time." graphql-js `buildSchema(source, options)` accepts only SDL and build options; schemas built that way have no field resolvers and fall back to `defaultFieldResolver`/`rootValue` at execute time.
findings.fix: Drop `buildSchema` from the sentence ("glued at `makeExecutableSchema` time"), or say "with bare `buildSchema` there is no resolver argument — you assign `field.resolve` yourself or pass `rootValue`".

findings.summary: The abstract-type resolution order is reversed: graphql-js's default type resolver checks `source.__typename` before it tries `isTypeOf`, so `__typename` is not the fallback after `isTypeOf`.
findings.evidence: "Or `isTypeOf` on each member type" / "Fallback is `source.__typename` if present". `defaultTypeResolver` starts with `if (isObjectLike(value) && typeof value.__typename === 'string') return value.__typename;` and only then iterates possible types calling `isTypeOf`.
findings.fix: Reorder to: "Interfaces and unions need `__resolveType`" → "Without one, the default resolver reads `source.__typename` first" → "Then falls back to `isTypeOf` on each member type".

findings.summary: Class getters are lumped in with methods as receiving `args`, but a getter's value is read, not called with the resolver arguments.
findings.evidence: "A class getter or method named `name` is invoked too" followed by "And why they receive `args` as their first parameter". `defaultFieldResolver` does `const property = source[info.fieldName]` — a getter has already run and returned a value at that point; only `typeof property === 'function'` triggers `property(args, contextValue, info)`.
findings.fix: Split the claims: "A getter named `name` is read like a property" and "A *method* named `name` is called — with `args` first, not `parent`".
